volume: 第一卷古艷部 Volume 1: Ancient Splendor Department

stories.title_en: Promote an official / Promotion of officials
stories.text: 一官陞職，謂其妻曰：「我的官職比前更大了。」妻曰：「官大，不知此物亦大不？」官曰：「自然。」及行事，妻怪其藐小如故，官曰：「大了許多，汝自不覺著。」妻曰：「如何不覺？」官曰：「難道老爺升了官職，奶奶還照舊不成？少不得我的大，你的也大了。」
stories.translation: An official, after being promoted, said to his wife: "My official position is now greater than before." His wife asked: "If the office is bigger, I wonder if this thing is also bigger?" The official said: "Of course." When it came to the matter, his wife found it as small as before and was surprised. The official said: "It has grown much bigger; you just don't notice." His wife asked: "How could I not feel it?" The official said: "If the master has been promoted to a higher position, how can the grandmother still remain the same?" "Without doubt, if mine is bigger, yours should be bigger as well."

stories.text: 甲乙兩同年初中。甲選館職，乙授縣令。甲一日乃驕語之曰：「吾位列清華，身依宸禁，與年兄做有司者，資格懸殊。他不具論，即選拜客用大字帖兒，身份體面，何啻天淵。」乙曰：「你帖上能用幾字，豈如我告示中的字，不更大許多？曉諭通衢，百姓無不凜遵恪守，年兄卻無用處。」甲曰：「然則金瓜黃蓋，顯赫炫耀，兄可有否？」乙曰：「弟牌棍清道，列滿街衢，何止多兄數倍？」甲曰：「太史圖章，名標上苑，年兄能無羨慕乎？」乙曰：「弟有朝廷印信，生殺之權，惟吾操縱，視年兄身居冷曹，圖章私刻，誰來怕你？」甲不覺詞遁，乃曰：「總之，翰林聲價值千金。」乙笑曰：「吾坐堂時，百姓口稱青天爺爺，豈僅千金而已耶？」
stories.translation: Jia and Yi were classmates in the same year of junior high school. Jia was selected for a post at the Han zhi (Hall Office), while Yi was appointed as county magistrate. One day, Jia boasted to him: "I hold a position in the Qinghua (Imperial Academy), and I reside within the palace. Compared with my senior of the same year who serves as an official in charge of local affairs, our qualifications are vastly different. Let alone other aspects; even when it comes to the size of the letter used for visiting cards, and one's status and dignity, they are as different as heaven and earth." Yi replied: "How many characters can you use on your visiting card? They are not as large as the characters in my official notices, which are much bigger. They are posted on public roads to inform and warn the people; no one dares to disobey, but my senior of the same year has no use for them." Jia asked: "Then, do you have golden gourds and yellow canopies to display your grandeur and dazzle others?" Yi replied: "My younger brother's staff clears the way, filling the streets; it is not just several times more than yours." Jia said: "The Tai Shi (Grand Historian) seal, with one's name inscribed in the imperial garden—could my senior of the same year not feel envious?" Yi replied: "My younger brother holds the imperial seal and has the power of life and death, which I control. Considering that you are in a cold department (a minor or obscure office), your seals are privately engraved—what person would fear you?" Jia, realizing he could not argue further, said: "In any case, the reputation and value of a Hanlin scholar is worth thousands of gold." Yi laughed and said: "When I sit in court, the people call me 'the Heavenly Official,' which is worth far more than just thousands of gold!"

stories.text: 一官新到任，祭儀門畢，有未燼紙錢在地，官即取一錫錠藏好。門子稟曰：「老爺，這是紙錢，要他何用？」官曰：「我知道，且等我發個利市看。」
stories.translation: An official newly appointed to office, after completing the ritual at the ceremonial gate, saw some unburned paper money on the ground and immediately took a tin ingot to hide it away. The gatekeeper reported: "Master, this is paper money; what use would you have for it?" The official said: "I know that. Just wait and see if I can make a profit from it."

stories.text: 有農夫種茄不活，求計於老圃。老圃曰：「此不難，每茄樹下埋錢一文即活。」問其何故，答曰：「有錢者生，無錢者死。」
stories.translation: A farmer found that his eggplants would not grow, so he sought advice from an old gardener. The old gardener said: "This is not difficult; just bury one coin under each eggplant tree, and it will grow." When asked why this was so, he replied: "Where there is money, life grows; where there is no money, it dies."

stories.text: 一官最貪。一日，拘兩造對鞫，原告饋以五十金，被告聞知，加倍賄托。及審時，不問情由，抽簽竟打原告。原告將手作五數勢曰：「小的是有理的。」官亦以手覆曰：「奴才，你講有理。」又以手一仰曰：「他比你更有理哩。」
stories.translation: An official was extremely greedy. One day, he summoned both parties for a hearing; the plaintiff gave him fifty catties of gold. Upon learning this, the defendant doubled his bribe to secure favor. When it came time for the trial, without asking about the circumstances, he drew a lot and beat the plaintiff. The plaintiff raised his hand in a gesture of five fingers and said: "I am in the right." The official also covered with his hand and said: "You wretch, you claim to be in the right." Then he turned his palm upward and said: "He is even more in the right than you are."

stories.text: 一官出朱票，取赤金二錠，鋪戶送訖，當堂領價。官問：「價值幾何？」鋪家曰：「平價該若干，今係老爺取用，只領半價可也。」官顧左右曰：「這等，發一錠還他。」發金後，鋪戶仍候領價。官曰：「價已發過了。」鋪家曰：「並未曾發。」官怒曰：「刁奴才，你說只領半價，故發一錠還你，抵了一半價錢。本縣不曾虧了你，如何胡纏？快攆出去！」
stories.translation: An official issued a red ticket to take two ingots of red gold. After the shop owner delivered them, he received payment on the spot in court. The official asked: "What is its value?" The shop owner replied: "At the regular price, it should be a certain amount. Since you, Master, are taking it now, I will only charge half price." The official looked at those around him and said: "In that case, give back one ingot to him." After the gold was given out, the shop owner still waited for payment. The official said: "The price has already been paid." łoż The shop owner replied: "It was never given to me." The official angrily said: "You cunning wretch, you said you would only accept half the price. Therefore, I gave back one ingot to you, which covered half of it." "This county has not wronged you in any way; how dare you纠缠 (persistently trouble) me?" "Get out quickly!"

stories.text: 一青盲人涉訟，自訴眼瞎。官曰：「你明明一雙清白眼，如何詐瞎？」答曰：「老爺看小人是清白的，小人看老爺卻是糊塗得緊。」
stories.translation: A blind person involved in a lawsuit claimed that he was blind. The official said: "You clearly have a pair of clear, white eyes; how can you pretend to be blind?" The man replied: "Master sees me as clear and innocent, but I see Master as extremely confused."

stories.text: 一官斷事不明，惟好酒怠政，貪財酷民。百姓怨恨，乃作詩以誚之云：「黑漆皮燈籠，半天螢火蟲。粉牆畫白虎，黃紙寫烏龍。茄子敲泥磬，冬瓜撞木鐘。唯知錢與酒，不管正和公。」
stories.translation: An official failed to adjudicate affairs properly, loved drinking and neglected government duties, was greedy for wealth, and harsh toward the people. The people resented him and composed a poem to mock him: "A black lacquered lantern, half the sky of fireflies. "White tigers painted on white walls, yellow paper writing about black dragons." "Eggplants striking clay chimes, winter melons bumping wooden bells. "He only knows money and wine; he cares nothing for justice or fairness."

stories.title_en: Submit a memorial to the throne
stories.text: 一官被妻踏破紗帽，怒奏曰：「臣啟陛下，臣妻羅皂，昨日相爭，踏破臣的紗帽。」上傳旨云：「卿須忍耐。皇后有些憊賴，與朕一言不合，平天冠打得粉碎，你的紗帽只算得個卵袋。」
stories.translation: An official, whose wife had trampled his gauze hat, angrily submitted a memorial saying: "I respectfully report to Your Majesty, my wife Luo Zao quarreled with me yesterday and trampled on my gauze hat." The emperor issued an edict: "You must endure this patiently. "The empress is somewhat stubborn; when she disagreed with me on a single word, her imperial crown was smashed into pieces. Your gauze hat is merely an egg bag."

stories.text: 有失牛而訟於官者，官問曰：「幾時偷去的？」答曰：「老爺，明日沒有的。」吏在傍不覺失笑，官怒曰：「想就是你偷了！」吏洒兩袖曰：「任憑老爺搜。」
stories.translation: A man reported to the official that he had lost a cow. The official asked: "When was it stolen?" The reply was: "Master, I found it missing tomorrow." A clerk nearby could not help but laugh secretly. The official angrily said: "I think you are the one who stole it!" The clerk flapped his sleeves and said: "Please search me as you wish."

stories.text: 官值暑月，欲覓避涼之地。同僚紛議，或曰某山幽雅，或曰某寺清閑。一老人進曰：「山寺雖好，總不如此座公廳，最是涼快。」官曰：「何以見得？」答曰：「別處多有日頭，獨此處有天無日。」
stories.translation: An official, during the hot summer months, wanted to find a cool place to escape the heat. His colleagues discussed it in groups; some said a certain mountain was quiet and elegant, while others recommended a particular temple for its peaceful seclusion. An old man stepped forward and said: "Although the mountains and temples are nice, they cannot compare to this office hall; it is the coolest of all." The official asked: "Why do you say that?" The reply was: "Other places have the sun, but here alone there is sky without sunlight."

stories.text: 一官素有清名，考察任滿，父老與之立德政碑告成。官命打轎往觀之，先於公厂坐下。少頃，左右稟曰：「請老爺看石同入碑同屄。」
stories.translation: An official who had long been known for his integrity was examined and found to have completed his term of office. The local elders erected a stele in honor of his virtuous governance, and the ceremony was concluded. The official ordered his sedan chair to be prepared so he could go view it, and first sat down at the public hall. After a short while, someone on his staff reported: "Please, Master, come see the stone same as entered stele same as bi."

stories.text: 鄉民初次入城，見有木桶懸于城上，問人曰：「此中何物？」應者曰：「強盜頭。」及至縣前，見無數木匣釘於譙樓之上，皆前官既去而所留遺愛之靴。鄉民不知，乃點首曰：「城上掛的強盜頭，此處一定是強盜腳了。」
stories.translation: A villager visiting the city for the first time saw a wooden bucket hanging on the city wall and asked someone: "What is inside this?" The person replied: "It's the head of a bandit." When he arrived in front of the county office, he saw countless wooden boxes nailed to the watchtower; they were all the leftover "loved boots" left behind by previous officials after their departure. The villager, not knowing this, nodded and said: "If the heads of bandits are hung on the city wall, then these here must certainly be the bandit's feet."

stories.text: 一官遇生辰，吏典聞其屬鼠，乃醵黃金鑄一鼠為壽。官甚喜，曰：「汝等可知奶奶生日，亦在目下乎？」眾吏曰：「不知，請問其屬？」』官曰：「小我一歲，丑年生的。」
stories.translation: An official celebrated his birthday. Upon hearing that he was born in the Year of the Rat, his clerks collected gold to cast a golden rat as a gift for longevity. The official was very pleased and said: "Do you know that my grandmother's birthday is also coming up soon?" The clerks replied: "We don't know. Please tell us what zodiac sign she belongs to?" The official said: "She is one year younger than me, born in the Year of Chou."

stories.text: 有妻妾各居者，一日，妾欲謁妻，謀之於夫：「當如何寫帖？」夫曰：「該用『寅弟』二字。」妾問：「其義何居？」夫曰：「同僚寫帖，皆用此稱呼，做官府之例耳。」妾曰：「我輩並無官職，如何亦寫此帖？」夫曰：「官職雖無，同僚仝屪總是一樣。」
stories.translation: There was a man with both a wife and concubine living separately. One day, the concubine wanted to visit her senior wife and asked her husband: "How should I write my visiting card?" Her husband said: "You should use the words 'Yin Di' (Junior Brother)." The concubine asked: "What is the meaning behind this?" Her husband replied: "When colleagues write visiting cards, they all use this title; it's just the official custom." The concubine said: "We are not officials and have no positions—why should we also write such a card?" Her husband replied: "Although we hold no official position, our status as colleagues Tong Jia is still the same."

stories.text: 官坐堂，眾役中有撒一響屁，官即叫：「拿來！」隸稟曰：「老爺，屁是一陣風，吹散沒影蹤，叫小的如何拿得？」官怒云：「為何徇情賣放，定要拿到。」皂無奈，只得取乾屎回銷：「稟老爺，正犯是走了，拿得家屬在此。」
stories.translation: An official was sitting in court when one of the attendants let out a loud fart. The official immediately shouted: "Bring him forward!" A clerk reported: "Master, a fart is just a gust of wind; it disperses and leaves no trace. How can I possibly catch it?" The official angrily said: "Why are you showing favoritism and letting him go? You must bring the culprit." The attendant had no choice but to take some dried feces and presented it, saying: "Reporting to Master, the main culprit has escaped, but we have captured a family member here."

stories.text: 一人最好古董，有持文王鼎求售者，以百金買之。又一人持一夜壺至，銅色斑駁陸離，云是武王時物，亦索重價。曰：「銅色雖好，只是肚裡臭甚。」答曰：「腹中雖臭，難道不是個周州仝銅同仝。」
stories.translation: A man was very fond of antiques. When someone came to sell a Wenwang Ding (tripod), he bought it for one hundred catties of gold. Another person came with a night pot, its copper color mottled and lustrous. He claimed it was an artifact from the time of King Wu and asked for a high price as well. He said: "Although the copper color is nice, its inside still smells very bad." The other replied: "Though it stinks in the belly, is it not still a Zhou Zhou Tong bronze Tong Tong?"

stories.text: 衙官聚會，各問何職。一官曰：「隨常茶飯掇將來，蓋義取現成縣丞同音也」一官曰：「滾湯鍋裏下文書，乃煮主仝音簿也。」一官曰：「鄉下蠻子租糞窖。」問者不解，答曰：「典屎史同音。」
stories.translation: Officials gathered for a meeting, and each asked about the other's position. One official said: "Bring tea and meals as usual—this means I take care of the ready-made Xian Cheng, same pronunciation as Xian Cheng." Another official said: "Put documents into a boiling pot—it means I handle the records Zhu Tong, similar pronunciation to Zhu Tong." One official said: "The villagers' manure pits from the countryside." The questioner did not understand, so he was told: "Managing excrement Shi, same pronunciation as Shi."

stories.text: 一作吏典者，有媳婦最善詳夢。適三考已滿，將往謁選。夜得一夢，呼媳詳之。媳問：「何夢？」公曰：「夢見把許多冊籍，放在鍋內熬煮，不知主何吉凶？」媳曰：「初選一定是個主簿。」隔數日，公曰：「我又得一夢，夢見你我二人皆裸體而立，身子卻是相背的，何也？」媳曰：「恭喜一轉，就是縣現丞成。」
stories.translation: There was a clerk whose daughter-in-law was especially skilled in interpreting dreams. At that time, after completing three terms of office, he was about to go for official selection. That night, he had a dream and called his daughter-in-law to interpret it for him. The daughter-in-law asked: "What was the dream?" He said: "I dreamed of putting many volumes of records into a pot and boiling them. I don't know what this signifies—good or bad?" The daughter-in-law said: "You must be appointed as a Zhubu (a minor official) in the first selection." A few days later, he said: "I had another dream. I dreamed that both you and I were standing naked, but our bodies were facing opposite directions. What does this mean?" The daughter-in-law said: "Congratulations! This means you will now be promoted to Xian (Xian) Cheng (Cheng)."

stories.text: 鎮守太監觀風，出「後生可畏焉」為題，眾皆掩口而笑。璫問其故，教官稟曰：「諸生以題目太難，求減得一字也好。」璫笑曰：「既如此，除了『後』字，只做『生可畏焉』罷。」
stories.translation: A eunuch in charge of guarding observed the situation and proposed the topic "The youth are to be feared," which made everyone laugh behind their hands. When the eunuch asked why, the instructor reported: "The students found the topic too difficult and are asking to have even one character removed." The eunuch smiled and said: "If that is the case, let us remove the character 'hòu' (after), and just write on 'shēng kě wèi yān' (the youth are to be feared)."

stories.text: 內相見人撒尿，喜甚，喚他過來一看。其人脫褲，見此物尚在攛動，內相拍掌大喜曰：「我的乖兒，見我公公，只消常禮兒罷了。」
stories.translation: An eunuch saw someone urinating and was very pleased, calling him over to take a look. When the man took off his pants and this thing was still moving, the eunuch clapped his hands in great joy and said: "My dear boy, upon seeing my uncle, you only need to perform a simple courtesy."

stories.text: 一遼東武職，素不識字。一日被論，使人念劾本云：「所當革任回衛者也。」因痛哭曰：「『革任回衛』還是小事，這『者也』二字，怎麼當得起！」
stories.translation: A military official from Liaodong had never learned to read or write. One day, he was impeached and had someone recite the indictment: "He should be stripped of his post and sent back to the garrison." He then wept bitterly, saying: "Being 'stripped of my post and sent back to the garrision' is still a small matter. How can I bear these two words, 'zhe ye'!"

stories.text: 一武弁夜巡，有犯夜者，自稱書生會課歸遲。武弁曰：「既是書生，且考你一考。」生請題，武弁思之不得，喝曰：「造化了你，今夜幸而沒有題目。」
stories.translation: One night, a military official was on patrol and encountered someone violating the curfew. The person claimed to be a scholar who had returned late after attending a study session. The military official said: "Since you are a scholar, let me test you for a moment." The scholar asked for the question. The military official, unable to think of one, shouted: "You've outwitted me! Fortunately, there was no question tonight."

stories.text: 一武官出征將敗，忽有神兵助陣，反大勝。官叩頭請神姓名，神曰：「我是垛子。」官曰：「小將何德，敢勞垛子尊神見救？」答曰：「感汝平昔在教場，從不曾有一箭傷我。」
stories.translation: A military officer was about to lose a battle when suddenly divine troops came to his aid, and he turned the tide into a great victory. The official kowtowed and asked for the deity's name, and the deity said: "I am Duozi." The officer said: "What virtue do I, a lowly soldier, possess to deserve your rescue, O revered deity Duozi?" The deity replied: "I was moved by the fact that in the past you never once shot an arrow at me during training sessions."

stories.title_en: Jinshi Street / House of a Jinshi Degree Holder
stories.text: 一介弟橫行於鄉，怨家罵曰：「兄登黃甲，與汝何干，而豪橫若此？」答曰：「你不見匾額上面寫著『進士第弟』麼？」
stories.translation: A younger brother was bullying the local villagers, and an enemy scolded him: "Your elder brother passed the imperial examination and became a Jinshi—what does that have to do with you? Why are you so arrogant and violent?" The younger brother replied: "Haven't you seen the plaque above that says 'Jinshi Di Di'?"

stories.text: 一舉子往京赴試，僕挑行李隨後。行到曠野，忽狂風大作，將擔上頭巾吹下。僕大叫曰：「落地了！」主人心下不悅，囑曰：「今後莫說落地，只說及第。」僕領之；將行李拴好，曰：「如今恁你走上天去，再也不會及第了。」
stories.translation: A candidate for the imperial examination was heading to the capital for the exam, with a servant carrying his luggage behind him. As they walked through an open field, suddenly a strong wind blew up and knocked the headpiece from the top of the luggage pole. The servant shouted: "It's fallen!" The master was displeased and instructed: "From now on, don't say 'it has fallen,' just say 'passed the examination.'" The servant understood. After securing the luggage, he said: "Now even if you were to run up into the sky, it will never pass again."

stories.title_en: A Poem Mocking a Military Examination Candidate
stories.text: 頭戴銀雀頂，腳踏粉底皂。也去參主考，也來謁孔廟。顏淵喟然歎，夫子莞爾笑。子路慍見曰：「這般呆狗醮，我若行三軍，都去喂馬料。」
stories.translation: On his head, he wore a silver sparrow cap; on his feet, black shoes with white soles. He also went to pay respects to the chief examiner and visited Confucius's temple as well. Yan Yuan sighed deeply, while Master Kong smiled gently. Zilu angrily remarked: "Such a foolish dog-like fellow—if I were to command the army, they would all be fed horse fodder."

stories.text: 有市井獲封者，初見縣官，甚跼蹐，堅辭上坐。官曰：「叨為令郎同年，論理還該侍坐。」封君乃張目問曰：「你也是屬狗的麼？」
stories.translation: There was a commoner who had been granted noble status. Upon his first meeting with the county official, he felt very uneasy and insisted on declining to sit in the upper seat. The official said: "I am honored to be your son's classmate from the same examination year; by etiquette, you should still sit in attendance." The noble lady then opened her eyes wide and asked: "Are you also a dog?"

stories.text: 一市井受封，初見縣官，以其齒尊，稱之曰：「老先。」其人含怒而歸，子問其故，曰：「官欺我太甚。彼該稱我老先生才是，乃作歇後語，叫甚麼老先，明係輕薄。我回稱，也不曾失了便宜。」子詢何以稱呼，答曰：「我本應稱他老父母，今亦縮住後韻，只叫他聲老父。」
stories.translation: A commoner who had received a noble title met the county official for the first time. Respecting his seniority, he addressed him as: "Old Sir." The official returned in anger. His son asked why, and the father said: "That official has insulted me greatly. He should have called me 'Lao Xiansheng' (Old Master). Instead, he used a phrase that sounds like the beginning of an idiom and said just 'Lao Xian,' which clearly shows disrespect." "When I returned home, I did not lose any advantage either," he added. The son asked what title to use, and the father replied: "I should have addressed him as 'Lao Fu Mu' (Old Parent), but now I also shortened it by omitting the final syllable and just called him 'Lao Fu' (Old Father)."

stories.title_en: A Noble Title for a Young Man
stories.text: 有公子兼封君者，父對子，乃欣羨不已。訝問其故，曰：「你的爺既勝過我的爺，你的兒又勝過我的兒。」
stories.translation: There was an aristocrat who had both the status of a noble and that of a young gentleman. When his father addressed him, he expressed endless admiration. When surprised by the reason and asked about it, he said: "Your grandfather has surpassed my grandfather, and your son also surpasses my son."

stories.text: 一人問：「公子與封君孰樂？」答曰：「做封君雖樂，齒已衰矣，惟公子年少最樂。」其人急趨而去，追問其故，答曰：「買了書，好送家父去上學。」
stories.translation: Someone asked: "Which is more enjoyable, being a young gentleman or holding the title of a noble?" The reply was: "Although it's pleasant to be a noble, one's age has already declined. Only being a young gentleman is the most enjoyable when you are still young." The person hurried away quickly. When he was chased and asked why, he replied: "I bought books so I can send my father to school."

stories.text: 贈納粟詩曰：「革車買得截的高，周子窗前滿腹包。有朝若遇高曾祖，煥乎其有沒分毫。」
stories.translation: A poem was presented in appreciation of a grain contribution: "With silver, I bought a high official title; Zhouzi's window is now full to the brim. If in the future I meet my ancestors of old, they will surely be proud and not miss a single detail."

stories.text: 一監生過國學門，聞祭酒方盛怒兩生而治之，問門上人者：「然則打歟？罰歟？鐓鎖歟？」答曰：「出題考文。」生即咈然曰：「咦，罪不至此。」
stories.translation: A student from the Imperial Academy passed by the gate of the National College and heard that the Minister of Rites was greatly angered at two students and punishing them. He asked a person at the gate: "So, are they being beaten?" Or is it just a punishment? "Or are they being shackled?" The person replied: "They're given a topic for an examination essay." Hearing this, the student immediately exclaimed in surprise: "Hey, their crime is not that serious!"

stories.title_en: Imprisonment in a Prison for Officials
stories.text: 一監生妻，屢勸其夫讀書，因假寓於寺中。素無書箱，乃喚腳夫以羅擔挑書先往。腳夫中途疲甚，身坐擔上。適生至，聞傍人語所坐《通鑒》，因怒責腳夫。夫謝罪曰：「小人因為不識字，一時坐了鑒監，弗怪弗怪。」
stories.translation: The wife of an Imperial Academy student repeatedly urged her husband to study, so he pretended to stay at a temple. Since he had no bookcase, he called a porter and had him carry the books in a silk pole before going ahead. The porter became very tired on the way and sat down with the pole across his lap. Just then, the student arrived and heard someone nearby mention that he was sitting on a copy of the "General Mirror." He became angry and scolded the porter. The porter apologized, saying: "It's because I am illiterate and sat on the mirror Jian, please don't be angry. Please don't be angry."

stories.text: 一監生娶妾，號曰京姐，妻妒甚。夫詣妾，必告曰：「京裡去。」一日，欲往京去，妻曰：「且在此關上納了紗著。」既行事訖，妻曰：「汝今何不往京！」生曰：「毧也沒有一些在肚裏，京裡去做甚麼！」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student took a concubine and named her Jingjie. His wife was extremely jealous. Whenever the husband visited his concubine, he would always say: "I'm going to the capital." One day, when he wanted to go to the capital, his wife said: "First, stay here and finish weaving this silk." After finishing the task, the wife asked: "Why are you not going to the capital now?" The student replied: "I don't have even a little bit of knowledge in my belly. What would I do at the capital!"

stories.text: 貧子途遇監生，忽然抱住兜耳一口。生驚問其故，答曰：「我窮苦極矣，見了大錠銀子，如何不咬些飛邊用用。」
stories.translation: A poor man met an Imperial Academy student on the road and suddenly embraced him, biting his ear. The student was startled and asked the reason, to which he replied: "I am extremely poor and wretched. Seeing a big ingot of silver, how could I not bite off some flying edges to use?"

stories.text: 監生應付入場方出，一故人相遇揖之，並揖路傍豬屎。生問：「此臭物，揖之何為？」答曰：「他臭便臭，也從大腸場裏出來的。」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student was about to enter the examination hall when an old acquaintance met him and bowed, also bowing to a pile of pig dung by the roadside. The student asked: "This stinky thing, why are you bowing to it?" He replied: "It may be smelly, but it also comes out from the large intestine examination hall."

stories.text: 一生賃僧房讀書，每日遊玩，午後歸房，呼童取書來。童持《文選》，視之，曰：「低。」持《漢書》，視之，曰：「低。」又持《史記》，視之，曰：「低。」僧大詫曰：「此三書，熟其一，足稱飽學，俱云低，何也？」生曰：「我要睡，取書作枕頭耳。」
stories.translation: A student rented a monk's room to study, but played around every day. After noon, when returning to the room, he would call his servant and ask for the books to be brought over. The servant held up "Wenxuan," looked at it, and said: "Too low." He then held up the "Book of Han," looked at it, and again said: "Too low." Then he took up the "Records of the Grand Historian," looked at it, and once more said: "Too low." The monk was greatly surprised and asked: "These three books, mastering even one of them would be enough to call oneself a learned man. Yet you say all are too low—why is that?" The student said: "I want to sleep; I just take the books as a pillow."

stories.text: 監生至城隍廟，傍有監平聲生案。塑監生娘娘像。歸謂妻曰：「原來我們監生恁般尊貴，連你的像，早已都塑在城隍廟裏了。」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student went to the City God Temple, where there was a case involving another Imperial Academy student nearby. They sculpted an image of the Imperial Academy Student Niangniang. He returned and said to his wife: "Originally, we Imperial Academy students are so noble; even your image has already been sculpted in the City God Temple."

stories.text: 城裡監生與鄉下監生，各要爭大。城裡者恥之曰：「我們見多識廣，你鄉裏人孤陋寡聞。」兩人爭辯不已，因往大街同行，各見所長。到一大第門首，匾上「大中丞」三字，城裏監生倒看指謂曰：「這豈不是丞中大？乃一徵驗。」又到一宅，匾額是「大理卿」，鄉下監生以「卿」字認作「鄉」字，忙亦倒念指之曰：「這是鄉裏大了。」兩人各不見高下。又來一寺門首，上題「大士閣」，彼此平心和議曰：「原來閣各士自大。」
stories.translation: A city-based Imperial Academy student and a rural Imperial Academy student each wanted to claim superiority. The city-dweller scornfully said: "We are well-informed and experienced, while you country folk are narrow-minded and ignorant." The two continued to argue until they went together onto the main street, each trying to show off their strengths. They came to the gate of a grand mansion, where an inscription read "Da Zhongcheng" in three characters. The city-based Imperial Academy student looked at it upside down and pointed, saying: "Isn't this clearly 'Chengzhong Da'?" It was a test indeed." They came to another house, where the plaque read "Da Liqing." The rural Imperial Academy student mistook the character "Qing" for "Xiang," and hastily turned it upside down, pointing at it and saying: "This is a big 'xiang' (village)." The two could not determine who was superior. Coming to the gate of another temple, they saw an inscription reading "Dashige." With mutual respect and agreement, they said: "Originally, each scholar is great."

stories.text: 一人往妓館打丁畢，妓牽之索謝，答曰：「我生員也，奉祖制免丁。」俄焉又一人至，亦如之。妓曰：「為何？」答曰：「我監生也。」妓曰：「監生便怎麼？」其人曰：「豈不知監生從來是白丁。」
stories.translation: A man went to a brothel and finished beating the "ding." A prostitute pulled him, demanding payment for her services. He replied: "I am a scholar, and according to ancestral regulations, I am exempt from 'ding' duties." Soon after, another person arrived and did the same. The prostitute asked: "Why?" He replied: "I am an Imperial Academy student." The prostitute said: "What's special about being an Imperial Academy student?" The man replied: "Don't you know that Imperial Academy students have always been commoners?"

stories.text: 一監生姓王，加納知縣到任。初落學，青衿呈書，得「牽牛」章。講誦之際，忽問：「那王見之是何人？」答曰：「此王誦之之兄也。」又問：「那王曰然是何人？」答曰：「此王曰叟之弟也。」曰：「妙得緊。且喜我王氏一門，都在書上。」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student surnamed Wang, who had bribed his way to the position of county magistrate, took office. When he first entered school, a scholar in blue robe presented him with a book containing the chapter "Qiantou." While discussing and reciting it, he suddenly asked: "Who is that Wang Jianzhi?" The answer was: "This is the elder brother of Wang Songzhi." He asked again: "Who is that Wang Yaran?" The answer was: "This is the younger brother of Wang Yuosou." He said: "That's very clever." "And I'm delighted that all of my Wang family are mentioned in the book."

stories.text: 有監生，穿大衣，帶圓帽，于著衣鏡中自照，得意甚。指謂妻曰：「你看鏡中是何人？」妻曰：「臭烏龜！虧你做了監生，連自字多不識。」
stories.translation: There was an Imperial Academy student wearing a large robe and a round hat. Looking at himself in the mirror, he felt very pleased. He pointed to his reflection and said to his wife: "Look, who is this person in the mirror?" The wife replied: "Smelly turtle!" "Pity that you became an Imperial Academy student, yet you don't even recognize your own name."

stories.title_en: The Imperial Academy Student Bowing to His Father
stories.text: 一人援例入監，吩咐家人備帖拜老相公。僕曰：「父子如何用帖，恐被人談論。」生曰：「不然。今日進身之始，他客俱拜，焉有親父不拜之理？」僕問：「用何稱呼？」生沉吟曰：「寫個眷侍教生罷。」父見，怒責之。生曰：「稱呼斟酌切當，你自不解。父子一本至親，故下一『眷』字。『侍』者，父坐子立也。『教』者，從幼延師教訓。生者，父母生我也。」父怒轉盛，責其不通，生謂僕曰：「想是嫌我太妄了，你去另換過晚生帖兒來罷。」
stories.translation: A man, following an example, entered the Imperial Academy and instructed his family to prepare a letter to pay respects to Old Xianggong. The servant said: "How can father and son use letters? I am afraid people will talk about it." The student replied: "Not quite." "Today marks the beginning of my advancement. I have paid respects to all guests; how could there be a reason not to pay respect to my own father?" The servant asked: "What title should be used?" The student hesitated and said, "Just write 'Juan Shi Jiaosheng' (a respectful term for a student)." When the father saw it, he angrily scolded him. The student said: "I carefully considered and chose an appropriate title; you just don't understand." Father and son are the closest of relatives, so I added the character "juan" (affectionate relation). "The term 'shi' means that when the father sits, the son stands." "The term 'jiao' refers to having a teacher educate and instruct since childhood." "And the character 'sheng,' means I was born by my parents." The father's anger grew even stronger, scolding him for being ignorant. The student said to the servant: "I suppose he thinks I'm too arrogant; you go and get another respectful letter instead."

stories.text: 一監生妻謂其孤陋寡聞，使勸讀書。問：「讀書有甚好處？」妻曰：「一字值千金，如何無益？」生答曰：「難道我此身，半個字也不值？」
stories.translation: The wife of an Imperial Academy student said he was narrow-minded and ignorant, and urged him to study. She asked: "What good is there in reading books?" The wife replied: "One character is worth a thousand gold, how can it be of no benefit?" The student answered: "Does that mean my whole body isn't even worth half a character?"

stories.text: 一監生臨終，謂妻曰：「我一生掙得這副衣冠，死後必為我殯殮。」妻諾。既死，穿衣套靴訖，惟圓帽左右欹側難帶。妻哭曰：「我的天，一頂帽子也無福帶。」生復轉魂，張目謂妻曰：「必要帶的。」妻曰：「非不欲帶，恨枕不穩耳。」生曰：「對門某醫生家藥攆槽，借來好做枕。」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student, on his deathbed, said to his wife: "I have worked hard all my life for this robe and hat; after I die, you must definitely give me a proper funeral." The wife nodded in agreement. After he died, they dressed him and put on his boots; the only problem was that the round hat kept tilting to one side and could not be properly fastened. The wife wept and said: "Oh my heavens, even a single hat I am unable to wear." The spirit of the deceased returned briefly, opened his eyes, and told his wife: "It must be worn." The wife said: "It's not that I don't want to wear it; it's just the pillow is unstable." The student said: "Borrow the medicine mortar from Doctor Mou's family next door; it will make a good pillow."

stories.text: 一監生姓齊，家資甚富，但不識字。一日，府尊出票，取雞二隻，兔一隻。皂亦不識票中字，央齊監生看。生曰：「討雞二隻，兔一隻。」皂只買一雞回話。太守怒曰：「票上取雞二隻，兔一隻，為何只繳一雞？」皂以監生事稟，太守遂拘監生來問。時太守適有公幹，暫將監生收入齋戒庫內候究。生入庫，見碑上「齋戒」二字，認做他父親「齊成」姓名，張目驚詫，嗚咽不止。人問何故，答曰：「先人靈座，何人設建在此？睹物傷情，焉得不哭。」
stories.translation: An Imperial Academy student surnamed Qi was very wealthy, but illiterate. One day, the local magistrate issued a notice requesting two chickens and one rabbit. The official's attendant also could not read the characters on the notice and asked Master Qi to look at it. The student said: "Requesting two chickens, one rabbit." The attendant only bought back one chicken to report. The governor became angry and said: "The notice requested two chickens and one rabbit; why did you only submit one chicken?" The attendant explained the situation with the Imperial Academy student, so the governor summoned him for questioning. At that time, the governor had official business and temporarily placed the student in the Zhaijie Ku (a place for fasting and repentance) to await investigation. The student entered the Zhaijie Ku and saw the two characters "Zhaijie" on a stone tablet. Mistaking them for his father's name, Qi Cheng, he opened his eyes in shock and amazement, weeping uncontrollably. People asked why this was happening, to which he answered: "Why is my ancestor's spirit tablet placed here?" Seeing the object stirred up emotions; how could I not cry?"

stories.text: 一秀才畏考援例，堂試之日，至晚不能成篇。乃大書卷面曰：「惟其如此，所以如此。若要如此，何苦如此。」官見而笑曰：「寫得此四句出，畢竟還是個附例。」
stories.translation: A scholar, fearing the examination and relying on precedent, arrived at the day of the hall test but could not complete a single essay by evening. He then wrote boldly on the front of his scroll: "Because it is like this, therefore it is like this." "If one wants to do so, why go through such trouble?" The official saw this and laughed, saying: "To write these four lines is still essentially following precedent."

stories.text: 小虎謂老虎曰：「今日出山，搏得一人，食之滋味甚異，上半截酸，下半截臭，究竟不知是何等人。」老虎曰：「此必是秀才納監者。」
stories.translation: Xiaohu said to the tiger: "Today when I went out of the mountain, I killed a person and ate him. The taste was very strange—the upper half was sour, and the lower half was smelly; in the end, I still don't know what kind of person he was." The tiger said: "This must have been a scholar who paid to become an official."

stories.text: 一生見有投制生帖者，深嘆「制」字新奇。偶致一遠札，遂效之。僕致書回，生問：「見書有何話說？」僕曰：「當面啟看，便問：『老相公無恙？』又問：『老安人好否？』予曰：『俱安。』乃沉吟半響，帶笑而入，纔發回書。」生大喜曰：「人不可不學，只一字用得著當，便一家俱問，到添下許多殷勤。」
stories.translation: A student saw someone submitting a petition for an official position through payment, and greatly admired the character "zhi" (制) as being novel. After receiving a letter from afar by chance, he imitated it. His servant wrote back a reply, and the student asked: "What did you say in your letter?" The servant said: "When I opened it face-to-face, the first question was: 'Is my old master well?'" Then he asked again: "How is your old lady?" I said, 'They are all well.' Then he pondered for a while in silence, smiled and went inside before finally sending back the reply letter." The student was greatly pleased and said: "One must not stop learning. Just using one character appropriately can lead to the whole family being asked about, adding much more warmth and courtesy."

stories.text: 一財主不通文墨，謂友曰：「某人甚是欠通，清早來拜我，就寫晚生帖。」傍一監生曰：「這到還差不遠。好像這兩日秋天拜客，竟有寫春（眷）生帖子的哩。」
stories.translation: A wealthy man who was illiterate said to a friend: "This person is very unrefined. He came to visit me early in the morning and yet wrote a 'wan sheng' letter." A student from the Imperial Academy nearby said: "This is actually not too far off." "It seems that in these past two days, during autumn visits to guests, there were even people writing 'chun (juan) sheng' letters."

stories.text: 有走柬借牛于富翁者，翁方對客，諱不識字，偽啟緘視之。對來使曰：「知道了，少刻我自來也。」
stories.translation: A person sent a note to borrow a cow from a wealthy old man. The old man, who was entertaining guests at the time and pretended not to know how to read, opened the sealed letter feigning ignorance. He said to the messenger: "I understand; I will come myself shortly."

stories.text: 孔子見死麟，哭之不置。弟子謀所以慰之者，乃編錢掛牛體，告孔子曰：「麟已活矣。」孔子觀之，曰：「非也，分明一隻牛，只多這幾個錢耳。」
stories.translation: Confucius saw the dead qilin and wept without ceasing. The disciples planned to comfort him, so they strung together coins and hung them on a cow's body. They told Confucius: "The qilin is already alive." Confucius looked at it and said, "No, this is clearly a cow; only several coins have been added to it."

stories.title_en: A Poem on the River Center
stories.text: 有富翁同友遠出，泊舟江中。偶散步上岸，見壁間題「江心賦」三字，錯認「賦」字為「賊」字，驚欲走匿。友問故，指曰：「此處有賊。」友曰：「賦也，非賊也。」其人曰：「賦（富）便賦了，終是有些賊形。」
stories.translation: There was a wealthy man who traveled far with his friend, mooring their boat in the middle of the river. While strolling ashore by chance, he saw the three characters "Jiangxin Fu" written on a wall. Mistaking the character "Fu" for "Ze," he was startled and wanted to run away and hide. His friend asked why, and he pointed and said: "There is a thief here." The friend said: "It's 'Fu,' not 'Ze.'" The man said, "Even if it is Fu (wealth), there are still some signs of a thief."

stories.text: 富翁與人論及童子多肖乳母，為吃其乳，氣相感也。其人謂富翁曰：「若是如此，想來足下從幼是吃乳餅大的。」
stories.translation: A wealthy old man was discussing with others that many children resemble their wet nurses, because by drinking their breast milk, the vital energies become connected. The person said to the wealthy old man: "If that is so, I suppose you must have been raised on breast milk cakes since childhood."

stories.text: 一鬼托生時，冥王判作富人。鬼曰：「不願富也。但求一生衣食不缺，無是無非，燒清香，吃苦茶，安閑過日足矣。」冥王曰：「要銀子便再與你幾萬，這樣安閑清福，卻不許你享。」
stories.translation: A ghost, when being reborn, was judged by the King of Hell to be born as a wealthy person. The ghost said: "I do not wish to be rich." "I only ask for a life without lacking food and clothing, free from disputes and blame, burning fragrant incense, drinking bitter tea, and living in peace and leisure is enough." The King of Hell said: "If you want silver, I can give you tens of thousands more. But such a peaceful and quiet life is not something I will allow you to enjoy."

stories.text: 一富翁問「薑」字如何寫，對以草字頭，次一字，次田字，又一字，又田字，又一字。其人寫草、壹、田、壹、田、壹，寫訖玩之，罵曰：「天殺的，如何誑我！分明作耍我造成一座寶塔了。」
stories.translation: A wealthy old man asked how to write the character "jiang," and was told: it starts with a grass radical, followed by one stroke, then the character tian, another single stroke, again the character tian, and finally another single stroke. The man wrote 草, 壹, 田, 壹, 田 and 壹 in sequence. After finishing, he examined it and cursed: "Heavens! How could you deceive me!" "It's clearly a trick to make me build a treasure pagoda!"

stories.text: 一富翁含銀于口，誤吞入腹，痛甚，延醫治之。醫曰：「不難，先買紙牌一副，燒灰咽之，再用艾丸灸臍，其銀自出。」翁詢其故，醫曰：「外面用火燒，裏面有強盜打劫，那怕你的銀子不出來！」
stories.translation: A wealthy old man had a piece of silver in his mouth and accidentally swallowed it, causing great pain. He invited a doctor to treat him. The doctor said: "It's not difficult. First, buy a set of playing cards, burn them into ashes and swallow them; then use mugwort pills to moxibust the navel, and the silver will come out by itself." The old man asked why this would work, and the doctor said: "Fire is used from outside to burn it, while inside there are robbers raiding. How could your silver not come out!"

stories.text: 一富人有餘田數畝、租與張三者種，每畝索雞一隻。張三將雞藏於背後，田主遂作吟哦之聲曰：「此田不與張三種。」張三忙將雞獻出，田主又吟曰：「不與張三卻與誰？」張三曰：「初間不與我，後又與我，何也？」田主曰：「初乃無稽（雞）之談，後乃見機（雞）而作也。」
stories.translation: A wealthy man had several extra acres of land, which he rented to Zhang San for cultivation, demanding one chicken per mu. Zhang San hid the chicken behind his back, so the landowner made a reciting sound and said: "This field will not be farmed by Zhang San." Zhang San hurriedly presented the chicken, and the landowner recited again: "If not given to Zhang San, then who else?" Zhang San asked: "Initially you wouldn't give it to me, and now you do. Why is that?" The landowner said: "Initially it was a baseless (chicken-less) talk, but later I acted upon seeing the chicken."

stories.text: 有姓李者，暴富而驕。或嘲之云：「一童子讀《百家姓》首句，求師講解。師曰：『趙是精趙的趙字（蘇語謂放肆曰趙），錢是有銅錢的錢字．孫是小猢猻的孫字，李是張三李四的李字。』又問：『倒轉可講得否？』師曰：『也得。』童曰：『如何講？』師曰：『姓李的小猢猻，有了幾個銅錢，就精趙起來。』」
stories.translation: There was a man surnamed Li who had suddenly become rich and arrogant. Someone mocked him by saying: "A child once read the first line of 'Baijia Xing' and asked his teacher for an explanation." The teacher said: "Zhao is the Zhao character meaning 'to act recklessly' (in Suzhou dialect, 'zhaosui' means to be unrestrained); Qian is the Qian character for copper coins; Sun is the Sun character for a little monkey; and Li is the Li in Zhang San Li Si." The child then asked: "Can it be explained backwards?" The teacher said, "Yes." The child asked: "How is it explained?" The teacher said: "A little monkey surnamed Li, having acquired a few copper coins, has become reckless and arrogant."

stories.text: 富翁子不識字，人勸以延師訓之。先學「一」字是一畫，次「二」字二畫，次「三」字三畫。其子便欣然投筆，告父曰：「兒已都曉字義，何用師為？」父喜之，乃謝去。一日，父欲招萬姓者飲，命子晨起治狀，至午不見寫成。父往詢之，子患曰：「姓亦多矣，如何偏姓萬。自早至今，才得五百畫著哩！」
stories.translation: The wealthy man's son was illiterate, and people advised him to hire a teacher to educate his son. The boy first learned that the character "yi" is written with one stroke, then "er" with two strokes, and "san" with three strokes. The son was delighted, put down his brush, and told his father: "I already understand the meaning of all characters; why do we need a teacher?" The father was pleased and dismissed the teacher. One day, the father wanted to invite someone surnamed Wan for a drink and ordered his son to get up early in the morning to prepare an invitation. By noon, he had not seen it written yet. The father went to ask about it, and the son complained: "There are so many surnames; why must he be surnamed Wan?" "From early morning until now, I've only managed to write 500 strokes!"
